content.title: Understanding the Jones Act: Key Facts, History, and Economic Impact
content.text: Key Takeaways The Jones Act mandates the use of U.S.-built and operated ships for transporting goods between U.S. ports to support the domestic shipping industry.The Act is considered protectionist and significantly increases shipping costs, especially impacting non-continental U.S. territories like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico.Waivers to the Jones Act can be granted in times of emergency, such as natural disasters, to ease supply issues. What Is the Jones Act? The Jones Act, a crucial component of U.S. maritime law since 1920, mandates American-made, owned, and operated ships for transporting cargo between domestic ports. This protectionist legislation was introduced to strengthen the U.S. shipping industry post-World War I, but it also brings economic ramifications, especially for non-continental U.S. territories like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico. The Jones Act is Section 27 of the Merchant Marine Act of 1920, which provided for the maintenance of the American Merchant Marine.1 The Trump administration is considering a 30-day waiver of the Jones Act in March 2026, citing national defense needs tied to the Iran war's disruption of oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.2 The waiver would allow foreign tankers to move petroleum products between U.S. ports to help ease surging fuel prices. The History and Impact of the Jones Act U.S. Senator Wesley Jones of Washington introduced the Act to give his state a shipping monopoly to Alaska. It was enacted by the United States Congress to stimulate the shipping industry in the wake of World War I.3 As a protectionist law, the Jones Act addresses maritime trade, including cabotage, or domestic shipping. The Act requires that goods shipped between U.S. ports be transported on ships built, owned, and operated by United States citizens or permanent residents. These rules raise shipping costs to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other non-continental U.S. areas reliant on imports.4 Important The Jones Act is a piece of protectionist legislation that considerably increases the costs of shipping goods between two U.S. ports. Objectives Behind the Jones Act The Act aimed to revitalize the depleted U.S. maritime shipping industry post-World War I.Support the shipping industry and prevent the United States from relying on foreign-built ships.The Jones Act creates jobs and business revenue, supporting 650,000 American jobs and generating $150 billion annually..5 Key Requirements of the Jones Act Ships transporting cargo between two U.S. ports must be owned by U.S.-based companies, with over 75% of the ownership stake held by U.S. citizens.At least 75% of a ship's crew must be U.S. citizens.The ships must be built and registered in the U.S.6 Conditions for Jones Act Waivers In the wake of a natural disaster, such as a hurricane, the Act may be waived to increase the number of ships that can legally supply goods to an affected area.7The Secretary of Defense can request waivers in the "interest of national defense" and there is a separate procedure for non-defense entities. In both cases, the final authority for a waiver is the Secretary of Homeland Security.8 Controversies Related to the Jones Act The Jones Act is said to affect Puerto Rico's economic and budgetary troubles through its impact on trade with the island. A 2024 Purdue University study estimated that the Jones Act imposes an annual welfare burden of $1.4 billion on Puerto Rico, equal to a 30.6% tariff on U.S. shipments to the island. The largest share falls on consumers, who bear about $692 million of that cost, or about $203 per person annually.9 The waiver of the Act was implemented in 2022 only after Hurricane Fiona hit Puerto Rico. The Biden administration allowed a non-U.S. flagged ship to transport fuel to Puerto Rico, following pressure to waive the rule in the face of a fuel shortage to ensure that citizens could run generators needed for electricity and the functioning critical facilities.10 Opponents hope that a repeal of the Act will result in decreased shipping costs, lower prices, and less strain on government budgets. Proponents of the act include states with owners of navy yards, defense firms, and shipping industries, as well as the longshoremen and other personnel who work in ports. In March 2026, the Jones Act drew renewed attention as the Trump administration considered a 30-day waiver to ease a fuel price spike caused by the Iran war's disruption of oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The administration said it was exploring the waiver "in the interest of national defense" to keep petroleum products and agricultural goods flowing freely between U.S. ports, particularly from Gulf Coast refineries to the more densely populated East Coast. Experts estimated the move could save East Coast motorists about 10 cents per gallon, though they cautioned that broader market forces could offset the benefit.11 How Does the Jones Act Affect Puerto Rico? One consequence of the Jones Act is that it requires U.S. shipping for cargo between Puerto Rico and the U.S. mainland, increasing the cost of development for the island's economy.6 How Does the Jones Act Affect Cruise Ships? While the Jones Act doesn't cover passenger vessels, a related law has a similar effect on cruise ships. Under the 1886 Passenger Vessel Services Act, a foreign ship can't transport passengers directly between two U.S. ports.12 This means that a foreign-flagged cruise ship (the vast majority of cruise ships) must include foreign ports in any itinerary that begins and ends in a U.S. port. This often results in confusion or even fines for passengers who disembark at ports that violate the Jones Act. How Long Can a Waiver of the Jones Act Be Implemented? In 2020, Congress eliminated the federal government’s authority to issue long-term waivers, except in circumstances where a waiver is required to “address an immediate adverse effect on military operations.” Waivers that do not meet that standard must be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.10 The Bottom Line The Jones Act, part of the Merchant Marine Act of 1920, regulates maritime commerce by mandating that goods transported between U.S. ports must be on U.S.-built, owned, and operated ships. It was enacted to boost the U.S. shipping industry post-World War I but has faced criticism for raising shipping costs, especially for U.S. islands like Puerto Rico and Hawaii. While supporters highlight its role in generating jobs and economic activity, critics argue that it contributes to higher prices and economic challenges.
